Nestling development in the Pileated woodpecker (Dryocopus pileatus) proceeds through a series of well-defined stages, beginning with the hatching of altricial chicks that are entirely dependent on parental care. The initial wet weight of a newly hatched nestling is quite modest at 11 grams [Ww0 = 11 grams], a value that reflects the substantial energetic investment yet to come from the parents during the brooding period. Over the first weeks of life, the nestlings gain mass rapidly as they are fed a diet of carpenter ants and wood-boring beetle larvae. By the time they are ready to fledge, the young birds have achieved a much more substantial mass. The age at fledging, marked by the time since birth at fledging, has been recorded at 24 days [tx = 24 days] under the typical thermal conditions of the nest cavity, which during the active brooding period is maintained at approximately 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. This rapid developmental timeline is typical of many cavity-nesting picids, where the insulated nest environment buffers against thermal extremes and allows for efficient growth.

The reproductive biology of the Pileated woodpecker is characterized by a single annual breeding event, with females laying a clutch of eggs that is relatively small for a bird of its size. Field observations consistently report that females produce between 3 and 8 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 3 and 8 eggs per clutch], with the modal clutch size being around four eggs. The species is strictly single-brooded, producing only a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year]. This modest annual reproductive output is typical of larger woodpeckers that invest heavily in parental care and defend large territories. The reproductive rate is influenced by the availability of suitable dead and decaying trees for cavity excavation, which can be a limiting resource in managed forests. Pairs will typically remain on the same territory for many years, reusing and enlarging cavities in successive seasons, which underscores the importance of mature forest stands with a high density of snags for the species' conservation and reproductive success.

At a body temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], sexual maturation in the Pileated woodpecker is a gradual process that extends across the first few years of life, with young birds often remaining in their natal territory for an extended period before dispersing to establish their own breeding territories. The time since birth at puberty, representing the onset of gonadal development and the ability to breed, is estimated to occur at 72 days after hatching [tp = 72 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. However, despite reaching physiological maturity at this early age, individuals typically do not attempt to breed until they have successfully secured a territory and a mate. The time since birth at first brood, marking the age at which a bird successfully produces its first clutch, is consequently much later, occurring at 354 days since birth [tR = 354 days since birth] at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. This delay between reaching puberty and actual first reproduction reflects the intense competition for high-quality nesting sites in mature forests, where suitable excavation substrates are often limited and hotly contested among individuals.

The complete life cycle of the Pileated woodpecker extends over a remarkably long period for a bird of its size, with individuals that survive the high mortality of the first year often enjoying considerable longevity. The maximum lifespan recorded for this species, under the normal physiological operating conditions of endothermy at 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], is approximately 13 years [am = approximately 13 years]. This extended lifespan is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival over high annual fecundity, a pattern common among large-bodied forest birds that invest heavily in territorial defense and parental care. The oldest documented individuals in the wild have been estimated from banding returns, though the secretive nature of the species in mature forests makes precise longevity data difficult to obtain. This long reproductive window allows individuals to compensate for their modest annual clutch size through many years of breeding activity, ultimately achieving a lifetime reproductive output that is competitive with species that produce larger clutches but have shorter lifespans.

Adult body mass in the Pileated woodpecker exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, with females typically attaining a larger ultimate size than males, a reversal of the pattern seen in many other woodpecker species. The ultimate wet weight for female individuals has been recorded at a substantial 364 grams [Wwi = 364 grams], making the female of this species one of the largest woodpeckers in North America. In contrast, the wet weight at birth, immediately after the altricial chick hatches from the egg, is a relatively small 28.9 grams [Wwb = 28.9 grams], representing only a fraction of the adult mass. The incubation period, which takes place in a cavity where the eggs are held at a stable 36 °C [T = 36 °C], lasts between 15 and 18 days (15-18 days) [ab = 15-18 days], depending on ambient conditions and the attentiveness of the incubating parent. This dramatic increase in body mass over the nestling and juvenile periods underscores the critical importance of the parents' provisioning role in the species' life history.
